Biofouling effects were modeled as shifts in the power coefficient curve, decreasing both optimal tip- speed ratio and maximum Cp based on experimental data. The RL agent uses flow velocity as state, damping coefficient as action, and instantaneous Cp as reward, following an epsilon-greedy exploration policy. Tested on a year-long Mississippi River flow profile with progressive biofouling growth modeled by a logistic function, the adaptive controller generated 0.92% more energy than a fixed optimal-TSR baseline by continuously adapting to the changing plant without requiring explicit biofouling measurement. The fault reconnaissance study evaluated failure mechanisms across six WEC subsystems: generator, power electronics, WEC body, mooring lines, seals, and PTO. Each failure mode was ranked for probability and severity, with costs quantified based on work time, crew, vessel costs, and lost revenue for a 100 kW reference device. Biofouling emerged as a high-risk item at $204,000/year due to marine growth causing up to 45% power reduction. PTO failures present $254,000/year risk due to system complexity and drydocking requirements. Corrosion was prevalent across components, with seal degradation at $96,000/year risk. Extreme sea states posed $169,000/year risk to mooring systems. The outcomes of Task 7 provide actionable insights for the marine energy community. They demonstrate the need for adaptive control strategies and robust modeling approaches that account for environmental degradation. The work has been disseminated through technical reports and conference presentations, including the 2024 American Control Conference, and offers a foundation for future research and industry adoption. 3 Introduction Task 7 of the project aimed to investigate the effects of marine growth and system faults on the performance and control of marine energy systems. The task was motivated by the need to improve the reliability and efficiency of wave and current energy converters operating in harsh ocean environments. The task was divided into three main efforts toward the deliverables: (1) modeling and simulation of biofouling effects on the RM3 Wave Energy Converter (WEC), (2) development of adaptive control strategies for the SHARKS Marine Current Turbine (MCT), and (3) a fault reconnaissance study to identify common failure modes in WEC systems. There are 6 deliverables for Task 7 • Deliverable 7.1.1: Report on marine growth modeling methods. • Deliverable 7.2.1: Report on marine growth impact on RM3 performance. • Deliverable 7.3.1 Report on list of components, modes, and threats most likely to result in a WEC fault or failure. • Deliverable 7.4.1: Report quantifying the difference in performance between model-based and model-free control in the presence of faults. • Deliverable 7.4.2: Submit journal or conference publication on model-mismatch and fault-tolerant control. • Deliverable 7.4.3: Report on most promising near-term avenues for adoption of Task 7 findings for the research and industrial community, by connecting to relevant current projects and research activity with other groups.
